options: High fever within 48 hours of surgery
Severe and escalating from the first day
Felt a pop or gush of fluid after coughing/straining

history.ask: Coughing, vomiting, or straining since surgery

red_flags: Sudden profuse serosanguinous ('salmon-colored') discharge or a visible bulge of bowel — abdominal wound dehiscence / burst abdomen; urgent surgical referral
Severe wound pain with rapidly spreading dusky skin, crepitus, or bullae in the first 48 hours — necrotizing surgical site infection; urgent surgical referral
High fever with hypotension or confusion — sepsis from the wound or a deep collection
A tense, rapidly expanding wound swelling with a falling blood pressure — active bleeding into the wound

Fever, unexplained tachycardia, distension, or ileus after bowel surgery with an innocent-looking wound — anastomotic leak or organ/space infection hiding under a normal incision; urgent surgical referral
exam: Expose and inspect the entire wound in good light, comparing against expected healing for the post-operative day
Mark the limit of any erythema and time it — spread on review separates progressing infection from resolving inflammation
Palpate along the wound for fluctuance (collection), a tense swelling (hematoma), or a soft fluid wave (seroma)
Note the discharge on the dressing: pus, blood, serous fluid, or salmon-colored peritoneal fluid
Feel deliberately for crepitus and look for dusky or blistering skin around the incision
With a sterile glove, gently assess an open segment for fascial integrity — whether the deep layer is intact decides superficial separation vs true dehiscence
Ask the patient to cough while you watch and palpate the wound — a bulge or impulse reveals a fascial defect
Record temperature, BP, and pulse — quantify the systemic response
Examine the abdomen for distension, tenderness away from the wound, and bowel sounds — an organ/space collection declares itself here, not at the skin
Screen the other fever sources of the post-operative patient: chest auscultation, calf tenderness, urine appearance, IV cannula and drain sites

investigations.why: Rising leukocytosis supports surgical site infection or a deep collection; a falling hemoglobin supports hematoma or ongoing bleeding
CRP should fall after post-operative day 2–3 — a secondary rise is the earliest objective sign of infection or collection and separates it from normal healing
Types the organism in an infected wound and distinguishes true infection from colonization of an open wound
Confirms bacteremia when deep or organ/space infection is suspected over a simple superficial one
Poor glycemic control underlies infection and dehiscence — and this may be the moment diabetes is first found
Deranged renal function and electrolytes accompany sepsis and ileus from a deep collection; near-normal values fit seroma and superficial infection
Separates hematoma from seroma from abscess under the incision, and looks for free fluid or a deep collection after abdominal surgery
Second-line — if organ/space infection is suspected (fever + ileus with an unimpressive wound) or ultrasound is inconclusive: localizes the collection before referral

Pain worsening after initial improvement
Intact deep fascia on gentle assessment
Fever with rising CRP after day 3
Deep wound pain and induration out of proportion to surface signs
Pus from the depth of the wound or a collection deep to the fascia on ultrasound
Swinging fever
Fever and ileus with a relatively innocent wound after abdominal surgery
Tenderness away from the incision, distension
Collection on ultrasound or second-line CT
Salmon-colored fluid gush around day 5–10, often after coughing or straining
Palpable fascial defect or visible bowel
Cough, vomiting, or straining plus poor-healing risk factors
Tense, bruised, painful swelling in the first 48 hours
Dark blood discharge; falling hemoglobin if significant
Echogenic collection on ultrasound, afebrile early
Painless fluctuant swelling with clear straw-colored fluid, typically after mastectomy, hernia repair, or wide dissection
No fever, normal CRP trend
Simple anechoic fluid on ultrasound
Small localized pustule or nodule centered on a suture point
